posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.content_md:
John, the basic idea of combining DCG and silver halide has already been investigated. It was documented by a Bulgarian group in *Optical and Quantum Electronics***14** (1982), pages 311-315. However, I don't think the silver and DCG were "combining" to produce some kind of cumulative index modulation. I believe the function of the silver was simply to increase the sensitivity of the DCG. (?) It's been a long time since I read that paper, though. Martin is also familiar with it.

The title is "Dichromated gelatin for volume holographic recording with high sensitivity. Part I" 

Here is the abstract:

"Dichromated gelatin would be the most suitable irreversible medium for holographic recording but for its low sensitivity. The efficiency of the photoinduced reduction of the chromium ion increases considerably if superfine grains of silver halide crystals are present in the layer. The light sensitivity achieved is about 10 times better than that of dichromated gelatin layers, obtained and processed in the conventional way."

I have been giving this some thought and I might as well indulge in my ignorance simply for the fact of understanding. Let's talk this through.

I thought AmDi was a reversal bleach when used with silver halide. That is, it attacks ONLY the exposed and developed silver and makes them soluble which is washed away. It does nothing to the unexposed Sliver Halide grains.

So in the process of making a Silver Halide and AmDi plate or soaking an already fabricated Silver Halide plate, the Silver Halide and the AmDi get along just fine. During the exposure the exposed regions of silver halide salt take on the property of being able to turn to straight silver in the developer while the unexposed silver halide just sits there. During the exposure the exposed regions of gel/AmDi start getting cross-linked and in the unexposed areas they do not get the cross-linked. When the hologram is placed into the developer (High ph), I would guess the exposed areas of silver halide crystals start to turn to silver, possibly get broken down (by the AmDi) and get washed out. The cross-linked gelatin in these areas does not get washed out. In the unexposed regions the silver halide salts remain but I guess some of the uncross-linked gelatin gets washed out. The AmDi is not getting broken down but only getting diluted due to the PH of the Developer being high. Now we rinse quickly, where a slight big more of uncross-linked gelatin gets washed out, and place into fixer. The fixer (Low PH) breaks down the AmDi and washes it out. Still a little more uncrossed gelatin gets lost.

So in the end, before drying do we have an equalization of densities? Silver Halide crystals being lost in the exposed and uncrossed gelatin being lost in the unexposed areas.

Now, instead let’s fix the hologram first. The fixer attacks the AmDi and removed it. Some unexposed uncross-linked get removed. The Silver Halide (exposed and unexposed) undergoes no change. We then develop the hologram and the exposed Silver Halide turns to silver and a little more uncross-linked gelatin is washed away. We then put the hologram in a rehalogenating bleach and the unexposed salts are washed away and so is some more uncrossed gelatin all in the same unexposed areas. The exposed silver is converted back to silver halide in the areas of cross-linked unwashed away gelatin. Now, does this mixture of Silver Halide and cross-linked gelatin have a higher index of refraction then Silver halide or cross-linked gelatin alone?

I hope some of this makes sense, and please do not hesitate to point out any weaknesses in these statements. Or am I totally out in left field?

This statement is not just really so John. As you know, the wonderful virtually unique way silver halide can be broken down by light relies on the formation of latent image atoms of silver being formed by light normally with sensitizing dyes involved. These freed silver atoms can then go on to infect the hole grain of thousands of AgBr ion-pairs when the plate is put in developer. The photosensitivity process is dependent on there being an easily available source of electrons present which can readily supply the silver ion Ag+ with its missing electron to make it “Ag0” ---the formula for that black metal. 

 In otherwords it needs a reducing environment to enable it to occur , the developer of course being a strong reducing agent . Dichromate (which becomes chromate in alkaline soln.but the same oxygen to chromium ratio is maintained), is as you know a powerful oxidant because each two chromium atoms only need 3 oxygens between them to form their strong very stable “chromium lll” arrangements and that leaves the other 4 dichromate oxygens with their missing electrons to go off and seize them back to form more energetically favourable bonds with organic substances, above all with those strongly reducing photographic developers, but they can also get electrons off silver metal, Ag0 to form Ag+ again. 

The most energetic form of silver metal is the latent image spec which is made up of just a few atoms. The slightest whiff of dichromate and those latent image specs are gone! ( to reform Ag+ again or perhaps more correctly never allow the formation of Ag0 metal in the first place). 

Quite by coincidence our photoscience archive plunderer Martin send me the following at the end of an email today. 

Martin

“P.S. Digging in those old French journals, Bulletin de la société française de photographie (put online at Gallica), I run into some articles that raised my curiosity. There was a description of a method of forming a silver halide emulsion under daylight. The magic ingredient said to allow that, was potassium chromate, which had been added early on to the emulsion. “

So the coexistence of dichromate/chromate and latent silver image is just not a goer and neither is the necessary developer for the silver possible in the presence of dichromate. You can introduce the dichromate after the silver development step to get the SHDCG effect of course and you and many of us have discussed this at length on this forum with Joe’s post of ? and earlier.

Jeff

Jeff, thank you for explaining this! So if I understand you correctly the AmDi would keep the Silver Ions specs (Ag0) from being produced at all during the exposure. That being said, I see then entire thought is bad.

Concerning your last post. I use Kodak Rapid Fixer with hardener. If I am reading the MSDS correctly the most abundant ingredient is Ammonium Thiosulfate. I am not a chemistry expert so I am not sure how this compares to sodium sulfite. Here is the link for my fixer from my web page. [http://www.sketchys.com/HoloPage/HoloFi ... er.jsp.rtf](http://www.sketchys.com/HoloPage/HoloFiles/Holography%20Safety/Material%20Safety%20Data%20Sheet/KodakRapidFixer.jsp.rtf)

I did play with what the effects of fixer were on the DCG plate. 

Here is a view of a DCG hologram that was fixed for a very short time, about 1/4 of how I usually do it. Subsequent processing was my normal processing. Rinse 5 min, 4 alcohol baths warm with the last being hot. The emulsion is facing the camera. [http://www.sketchys.com/Holograms/Multi ... ulSide.jpg](http://www.sketchys.com/Holograms/MultiBeam/HalfFixEmulSide.jpg)

Here is a photo of the exact plate as seen from looking from the glass side. It seems the fixer penetrated but not enough to go all the way through the film. It is very milky almost opaque from the back. [http://www.sketchys.com/Holograms/Multi ... ssSide.jpg](http://www.sketchys.com/Holograms/MultiBeam/HalfFixGlassSide.jpg)

Finally, this is a plate that I soaked half the plate in the fixer for the normal time and the other half had no fixer at all (I kept it out of the fixer/hardener). [http://www.sketchys.com/Holograms/Multi ... fNoFix.jpg](http://www.sketchys.com/Holograms/MultiBeam/HalfNoFix.jpg)

Both plates were rinsed for 5 minutes in running water and processed in alcohol the same. I wanted to see if water alone could be used but it seems that to get red of milkiness the fixer with hardener is needed. Now, I am not sure if it is the hardener or the fixer that gets rid of the milkiness or if the rinse without fixer/hardener needs to be prolonged to a much longer time. But with my normal processing, fixer with hardener is needed or milkiness appears.

Things I have found that effect milkiness are; the length of time and concentration in the fixer/hardener, alcohol bath temperatures, Side of plate exposed and viewed, emulsion thickness and concentration of gelatin in emulsion.

I am not sure if these are all results of a single factor or not. Example; thicker emulsion or emulsions with higher gelatin concentration need to be fixed longer???

I did get a session in which I was struggling with milkiness, really bad, but only on the glass side of the emulsion. I tried fixing longer, I added more hardener, I rinsed longer but still the translucent milkiness was very evident on the glass side of the plate. I thought the fixer was not penetrating far enough as in my examples above. The strange thing is that the emulsion side of the plate was just fine. So after struggling for a while and trying different things I simply flipped the plate around (emulsion toward reference beam in a single beam reflection) in the exposure set up, and processed, thus the real image was viewable while looking directly at the emulsion side and not through the glass. This produced an acceptable hologram.

Here are some more effects of emulsion side vs. glass side viewing. This was an effect with all alcohols being very hot. Especially the first alcohol bath. I think this caused a differential swelling/shrinking of the fringes that were at the surface of the emulsion (thus white replay) but left the fringes the same size deeper in the emulsion. 

This is viewing through glass side.

[http://www.sketchys.com/Holograms/011005/LightHouse.JPG](http://www.sketchys.com/Holograms/011005/LightHouse.JPG)

This is viewing through emulsion side of the same exact hologram.

[http://www.sketchys.com/Holograms/01100 ... Pseudo.JPG](http://www.sketchys.com/Holograms/011005/LightHousePseudo.JPG)

DCG can keep you busy for a long, long time if you want to change variables. There are enough side trails for a life time. I think that's why I love it so much, I might enjoy the experimentation and seeing the different effects more then the actual finished holograms anymore.

Sorry to go on and on and I hope it addressed you question to some extent.

Peace!

John, your information is really useful, I have added it to my DCG folder by pasting your pics into a word file and pasted bits of your post for the legends under each pic. 

(But I was just not able to download your first pic).

I can see that through analyzing our different approaches that we (“we”=you,me, and hopefully other forum folk) can get more insight into the challenges of DCG than we could get going it alone.

An obvious item to me that makes rationalizing DCG processing more difficult is the use of proprietary fix/hardner and not knowing which is doing what, as you say yourself.

Would hardener alone have given you those results in your pics? If so then what hardener? If one goes for chrome alum hardener then one is of course competing with the primary process from the exposed dichromate for mainly carboxylic acid sites to crosslink along the polypeptide chain. If one goes for aldeyde hardening then one has most of the –NH2 sites along the chains available (but aldehydes like to get themselves oxidized by any unwashed out dichromate ions around).

 The “fix” bit can be a real complication but only if you have an initial high unreacted dichromate level around that can oxidize it thus forming chromium lll crosslinker. Is it really needed? 

I wonder if I have an answer to the above bit of your post by plugging in my experience over 15 years ago using soft gelatin with the lowest degree of hardness bias to avoid the use of hot alcohol baths and fire risk. So I was working at the other end of the hardness-bias range so to speak.

The key to the answer may be in the last sentence here taken from a paragraph from my paper in Applied Optics 30, 1589-1602 (1991)

…………..It is very helpful to keep the following mechanical model in mind. If one hangs weights on to the end of a steel extension spring, then removing those weights will result in the spring recovering its original un-extended length unless the weight exceeds a critical value. When a weight is of that critical value, the material of the spring has reached just beyond what is known as the "yield point". When that weight is removed the spring would normally never completely recover its original un-extended length but will remain permanently distorted. Had the material of the spring been a little stiffer, then that particular weight would not have stretched the spring beyond its yield point. If the temperature of the stiffer spring were to be raised however, then that weight may again take the spring beyond its yieldpoint.

DCG in water behaves similarly to the stretched spring. At a certain temperature, the stretching forces due to swelling in water may take the gelatin beyond its yield point. Had the water temperature been lower, then the gelatin would not have reached its yield point.

The art of making the most noise-free and yet bright DCG holograms, is to take the gelatin as close as possible to its yield point without exceeding it. Stretching gelatin beyond its yield point creates noise in the finished hologram. Using the onion layer analogy of Curran and Shankoff, the holographic fringe layers might resemble dried out onion with crinkled-up layers if the yield point is exceeded. A sign that you have got the swelling just right is no milkiness in the exposed area but milkiness in the unexposed area.

Do you think that there may have been a fairly precise critical exposure level needed in your film then and below that level you got milkiness? What was your object? Was it returning a good bit of light, or was it diffusing it?(in which case my idea likely to be wrong). So the light returning strongly from a nice flat bright object creates strong fringes with the reference beam in the film closest to the object.

By their nature the bright fringes may have actually had MORE light intensity than the reference beam light that first passed through the glass. (Ignoring the serious attenuation, the intensity would be technically DOUBLED at the cost of the zero intensity in the dark fringes.)

 So could the reference beam light inspite of being gradually attenuated by DCG absorbance have actually been sufficiently intensified next to the object to take you above that critical exposure level while the reference beam intensity at the glass interface just fell below that level? Hence the phenomenon you got. (I have seen that effect myself too).

Jeff
